Day 1, tick 29 (7:25am): The Iron Brigade drives Archer's brigade back across the Willoughby Run. Brigadier General James J. Archer is captured, brought in by Private Patrick Maloney of Company G, 2nd Wisconsin, who is killed later in the day. Doubleday reports nearly 1,000 prisoners from Archer's brigade; Heth says Archer fell into the enemy's hands with some 60 or 70 of his men.

Day 3, tick 483 (7:20am): COLGROVE'S CHARGE. After about two hours of sharpshooter fire from daylight, with the firing on his left receding, Colonel Colgrove is told to advance; across the 100-yard open meadow in front of the Confederate breastworks he sends the 2nd Massachusetts and the 27th Indiana at the double-quick. The 2nd Massachusetts loses about 130 and the 27th Indiana 112, the regiment commander Lieutenant Colonel Mudge among the killed; the 27th is called back behind the works and the Confederates' counter-charge is broken by the fire of the Union works. // Contested: the hour (Colgrove's report puts it about two hours after daylight; Williams says forenoon; others later). Mudge's reported last words, 'It is murder, but it is the order', come from survivors' later accounts, not the Official Records.

Day 1, tick 50 (9:10am): The XI Corps comes up through Gettysburg. Howard takes command of the field and Schurz of the corps, with Schimmelfennig leading Schurz's division. Barlow's First Division and Schimmelfennig's Third march through the town and deploy north of it on the I Corps' right, in position by about 2 p.m., with Steinwehr's division held on Cemetery Hill as a reserve. Barlow advances his whole line onto the rise known as Blocher's (Barlow's) Knoll, losing touch with the Third Division.

Day 3, tick 452 (5:05am): Johnson's Confederate division counterattacks to retain the breastworks. Stonewall Brigade, Jones, Nicholls, Steuart assault the XII Corps line. Greene's brigade and returning XII Corps units resist along the hillside works.

Day 3, tick 650 (6:40pm): Evening of July 3: the battle is over. The Official Records give the Union loss for the campaign as 23,049 in the revised return (3,155 killed, 14,529 wounded, 5,365 captured or missing) and the Confederate loss as 20,451 as returned (2,592 killed, 12,709 wounded, 5,150 captured or missing), a return the editors call approximate; later estimates run higher, the National Park Service giving about 23,000 and 28,000. // Contested: Confederate losses (20,451 as returned; Livermore's estimates about 28,000). The sum of 51,000 is the Park Service's rounded estimate, not an Official Records figure. The heavy rain is better attested for July 4.
Day 3, tick 547 (11:50am): Kemper, commanding the right of Pickett's division, is dangerously wounded; Colonel Mayo succeeds to his brigade.

Day 3, tick 542 (11:25am): On the left of the Confederate line Brockenbrough's Virginia brigade is the first to give way under flanking fire from the Union skirmishers and the artillery on that flank, exposing Pettigrew's left.

Day 3, tick 453 (4:25am): Lee and Longstreet meet on the morning of July 3. Longstreet has given orders for an attack by his right to pass around the hill held by the Union left; a few moments later Lee joins him and orders a column of attack from Pickett's, Heth's and part of Pender's divisions directly at the enemy's main position on Cemetery Hill. Longstreet writes that the distance to be crossed under fire seemed to him too great to insure great results, particularly as two-thirds of the troops had been in a severe battle two days earlier. // The remark that no 15,000 men could take the position is quoted from Longstreet's postwar memoirs, not from his report (OR 27/2 p.359).

Day 1, tick 60 (10:00am): Coster's brigade, left alone north of the town, is struck on three sides. The Official Records count 597 casualties in the brigade for the whole battle: 134th New York 252, 154th New York 200, 27th Pennsylvania 111, 73rd Pennsylvania 34; most were killed, wounded or captured in this fight.

Day 3, tick 524 (1:35pm): At 1:40 p.m., seeing Union guns limbered up and withdrawn, Alexander writes again: "For God's sake come quick. The 18 guns have gone. Come quick or my ammunition will not let me support you properly." // Text from Alexander's memoir (1907). The words once shown here, 'I would not make the charge now', do not appear in it.

Day 1, tick 64 (10:20am): Pender's division (Perrin's, Lane's, Thomas's and Scales's brigades) comes up against the I Corps' line on McPherson's and Seminary Ridges. Perrin's South Carolinians carry the ridge near the seminary; Scales is wounded and his North Carolina brigade is hit hard, the Confederate return counting 424 killed and wounded in it.

Day 3, tick 505 (8:30am): Heth's division under Pettigrew, in two lines, and part of Pender's division under Trimble (Lane's and Scales's brigades) are posted on Seminary Ridge on Pickett's left; Wilcox's brigade is ordered to move in rear of Pickett's right flank. // No Confederate count of the column appears in the reports read; Hancock estimated the attackers at more than 15,000 (OR 27/1 p.373).

Day 2, tick 304 (11:30am): Wilcox's advance halted. Reinforcements close the gap on Cemetery Ridge. Wright's Georgia brigade briefly breaks through Cemetery Ridge north of Wilcox but is driven back without support.

Day 1, tick 35 (7:55am): Davis's brigade presses Cutler's retiring regiments. Part of the 2nd and 42nd Mississippi shelter in the unfinished Railroad Cut north of the pike. Hall's battery, with no infantry left beside it, loses horses and a gun and falls back by sections along the railroad grading.

Day 3, tick 555 (12:30pm): The Confederate penetration is broken. Armistead's men streaming back over the wall or surrendering. Devereux's 19th Massachusetts and others pour into the breach. The Angle is secured.

Day 2, tick 298 (11:00am): SICKLES IS WOUNDED. A cannon shot takes off his right leg near the Trostle farm and he is carried from the field; Birney takes command of the III Corps. // The story that Sickles smoked a cigar as he was carried off is a tradition, not in the Official Records.

Day 1, tick 52 (9:20am): Rodes sends Iverson's brigade forward and gives O'Neal the order to attack in person. O'Neal's brigade goes in with only three of its regiments, in confusion and not in the direction Rodes ordered; the 5th Alabama, held back by Rodes himself as a reserve, is sent in too late, and O'Neal, instead of leading, has stayed with it. The brigade is repulsed quickly.

Day 3, tick 548 (11:55am): On the left of the point of attack the Confederate lines of Pettigrew's division meet Hays's division and the troops posted in its extreme front and right; mowed down by Woodruff's canister and musketry, they break in great disorder, leaving fifteen colors and nearly 2,000 prisoners in Hays's hands.

Day 2, tick 258 (7:40am): Hood is severely wounded soon after getting under fire and leaves the field; Law takes the division. Brigadier General G. T. Anderson is also severely wounded. // Hood's later claim that he asked to swing around Big Round Top is not in the Official Records.

Day 3, tick 556 (12:35pm): Along the line the assault gives way; the survivors fall back toward Seminary Ridge. Lee's report says the troops were rallied and re-formed and that the enemy did not pursue. Pettigrew and Trimble are wounded. // The words 'It is all my fault', reported from Lee as he met the survivors, come from witnesses' later accounts, not the Official Records.

V-021 "Farnsworth's Charge" (tick 568): About 5 p.m. on July 3 Kilpatrick ordered Farnsworth's brigade to charge on the Confederate right south of the Round Tops, and Farnsworth was killed leading it. Farnsworth had been a brigadier general since June 29. Reports that he protested, and the words said to have passed between him and Kilpatrick, come from survivors' later accounts.

V-022 "Mudge and the Charge at Culp's Hill" (tick 483): On the morning of July 3 Colonel Colgrove sent the 2nd Massachusetts and the 27th Indiana across the open meadow in front of the Confederate breastworks on Culp's Hill. The 2nd Massachusetts lost about 130 killed and wounded, including its commander, Lieutenant Colonel Mudge, and the 27th Indiana 112. The hour is disputed and Mudge's reported last words come from survivors' later accounts.

V-019 "Pickett's Return" (tick 557): After the repulse Pickett's division came back across the fields. The Confederate return counts 2,888 casualties in it, 1,499 of them captured or missing (OR 27/2 p.339); Lee reports that Armistead and Garnett were killed and Kemper dangerously wounded. Pickett's remark that he had no division is a tradition from later accounts.

V-002 "Reynolds Falls" (tick 28): Major General John F. Reynolds, commanding the left wing of the Army of the Potomac, was killed on the morning of July 1 as the Iron Brigade went into McPherson's (Herbst) Woods. Doubleday gives the hour as about 10:15 a.m., Howard's reports give 11:15, and the source of the shot is unsettled.

V-023 "Lee Meets His Men" (tick 556): As the survivors of the assault came back toward Seminary Ridge, Lee rode out to meet them. Lee's report says the troops were rallied and re-formed and the enemy did not pursue. The words reported from him, such as 'It is all my fault', come from witnesses' later accounts, among them Imboden's postwar article.

V-012 "The First Minnesota" (tick 302): With Confederate columns reaching the gap in the line on July 2, Hancock ordered Colonel Colvill's 1st Minnesota to take the enemy's colors, wanting to gain time until reinforcements came up. The regiment charged and drove the enemy back. Fox counts 262 engaged and 224 casualties, nearly all in this fight, none missing; 215 were killed or wounded on July 2 itself, the highest percentage of any Union regiment in a single battle in his tables.

V-015 "Alexander's Two Messages" (tick 521): Colonel E. P. Alexander, Longstreet's artillery chief, sent two notes to Pickett during the cannonade, by his own later account at 1:25 and 1:40 p.m. The first said Pickett must come at once if he were to advance at all; the second, after Alexander saw Union guns withdraw, said 'For God's sake come quick.' The texts come from Alexander's memoir; the Official Records do not print them.

V-018 "Cushing's Battery" (tick 553): Lieutenant Alonzo Cushing commanded Battery A, 4th U.S. Artillery (six 3-inch rifles) at the Angle. Webb reports that he fought for an hour and a half after reporting that he was wounded in both thighs, and was killed at the fence by the side of his guns; Hunt lists him among the battery commanders killed. He was awarded the Medal of Honor in 2014.

V-013 "Greene's Lone Stand" (tick 315): When most of the XII Corps was sent to the left on July 2, Greene's brigade of five New York regiments (74 officers and 1,350 men by Geary's count, 1,424 in all) held the entrenched Culp's Hill alone against Johnson's division, which attacked about two hours after the opening on the right; Greene was reinforced during the evening by detachments from the I and XI Corps.

V-011 "Bigelow's Last Stand" (tick 300): The 9th Massachusetts Battery (six 12-pounder Napoleons), supporting the III Corps, covered the withdrawal of the batteries on its right and then retired by prolonge, firing as it went, to a position near two stone walls at the Trostle farm, which it was ordered to hold at all hazards without infantry support. It lost 8 killed, 17 wounded and 2 prisoners, and four of its guns were left in the field and recovered the same day, while McGilvery formed a line of guns behind it.
McPherson's Ridge: First major defensive position July 1. Buford's dismounted cavalry then Reynolds's I Corps. Iron Brigade charged into Herbst Woods from this ridge. (elevation 570 ft)

Little Round Top: Key terrain on Union left. Vincent's brigade arrived just in time July 2. 20th Maine held the extreme left. O'Rorke charged without orders. Hazlett dragged guns up the slope. (elevation 650 ft)
Lee's Headquarters: Near the Chambersburg Pike on Seminary Ridge.
Benner's Hill: Latimer's Confederate battalion placed here July 2. Badly cut up by Union counter-battery fire. Major Joseph Latimer, aged 19, was mortally wounded. (elevation 610 ft)
Mummasburg Road: Connects to Oak Ridge area. Used by Rodes for positioning.

The Wheatfield: John Rose's wheatfield. Fought over by several Confederate and Union brigades on July 2; it changed hands several times. The casualty total often quoted for the field is not given in the Official Records. (elevation 570 ft)

Oak Ridge: Baxter's ambush destroyed Iverson's brigade here. Paul's brigade fought here; Paul and several of the colonels who succeeded him were wounded. Iverson's dead were buried on this ground. (elevation 600 ft)

Barlow's Knoll: XI Corps right flank. Barlow was wounded here. Gordon's attack struck this position. Wilkeson's battery (G, 4th U.S.) was overrun here and Lieut. Wilkeson was mortally wounded. (elevation 550 ft)

Story marker "15th Alabama — Col. Oates attacked the left of the 20th Maine repeatedly; Oates later wrote that he made several assaults (the count of four and the story of the company sent for water are from his postwar account, not the reports)" (tick 268)

Tour stop 16 "Confederate Avenue" (The Retreat — July 4-5, 1863; tick 610): On the night of July 4-5, 1863, the Army of Northern Virginia began its retreat toward Virginia. A long wagon train of wounded men (Imboden's postwar account puts it at 17 miles) moved through driving rain toward the Potomac crossing at Williamsport. Meade chose not to pursue aggressively. President Lincoln was deeply disappointed that Lee's army escaped across the Potomac; in a letter to Meade that he did not send he wrote that Lee had been "within your easy grasp". Lee's army crossed the swollen Potomac on July 14, escaping to Virginia. The Gettysburg campaign was over. Estimated casualties: about 28,000 Confederate and about 23,000 Union (the Official Records return counts 20,451 and 23,0

Tour stop 12 "The Angle" (The High-Water Mark — July 3, about 3:30 PM; tick 549): About 3:30 PM on July 3 the survivors of the mile-long advance reached the stone wall at The Angle. By tradition Armistead raised his hat on his sword and called, "Come on, boys, give them the cold steel!" — words from survivors' later accounts. Led by Armistead, a part of his brigade crossed the wall and reached the guns of Cushing's battery. Lieutenant Alonzo Cushing, wounded in both thighs, had fought on for an hour and a half and was killed at the fence by his guns, Webb reports. Armistead fell wounded at the guns and was left within the Union lines, Harrow reports. A later account says that, told his old friend Hancock was wounded, he asked that his watch and effects be given to Hancock

Tour stop 11 "Cemetery Ridge" (Wright's Breakthrough — July 2, 7:30 PM; tick 315): In the fading light of July 2, Ambrose Wright's Georgia brigade achieved what no other Confederate force managed that day: Lee's report says Wright gained the crest of the ridge itself. Lee reports that Wright, having become separated from McLaws and gone beyond the other brigades of his division, was attacked in front and on both flanks and compelled to retire, unable to bring off any of the captured artillery. Hancock rushed every available man to seal the breach. The crisis passed. Whether the fight shaped Lee's decision to attack the center the next day is a matter of interpretation.
Story marker "72nd PA — Webb's Philadelphia Brigade held The Angle against Pickett's Charge (the 72nd stood behind the crest; the 69th and 71st held the wall)" (tick 548)

Tour stop 10 "Culp's Hill" (The Overnight Fight — July 2-3; tick 380): While the fighting raged on the Union left on July 2, Johnson's Confederate division attacked the right flank at Culp's Hill. Greene's New York brigade — 1,424 men by Geary's count, reinforced during the evening by detachments of the I and XI Corps — held the entrenched hill against Johnson's division. Greene's men benefited from the solid earthworks they had constructed, firing from protected positions while Confederate attackers struggled uphill through dense woods in darkness. The fight continued sporadically through the night. The XII Corps, back from the left, fought at daylight on July 3 to retake the works the Confederates held. Tour stop 7 "The Wheatfield" (Six Times Contested — July 2, afternoon and evening; tick 275): The Wheatfield of farmer George Rose became one of the bloodiest patches of ground in the battle on the afternoon and evening of July 2. By the usual count the field changed hands six times. Kershaw's South Carolina brigade attacked through Rose's Woods. de Trobriand's brigade and then Sweitzer's formed successive defensive lines. Caldwell's entire II Corps division — all four brigades under Cross, Kelly, Zook, and Brooke — countercharged through the field. Brigadier General Samuel Zook was mortally wounded leading his brigade into the fight. Colonel Patrick Kelly's Irish Brigade advanced; regimental tradition says the men wore green sprigs of boxwood in their caps. By nightfall the field wa

Story marker "Armistead fell here at Cushing's guns about 3:35 PM July 3 and was left mortally wounded within the Union lines (Harrow). Later accounts say he asked that a message and keepsake go to Hancock; that is tradition" (tick 551)

Tour stop 4 "Seminary Ridge" (The Union Retreat — July 1, 4:00 PM; tick 72): By mid-afternoon on July 1, the Union position north and west of Gettysburg had become untenable. The XI Corps was streaming back through the town in disorder, and the I Corps' right flank was exposed. The survivors rallied on Cemetery Hill south of town, where Howard had left Steinwehr's division as a reserve. The high ground — Cemetery Hill, Culp's Hill, and the long spine of Cemetery Ridge — would become the Union fishhook line that determined the battle's outcome. General Hancock arrived on Meade's order (3 p.m. by his own report, 4 p.m. by Howard's) and helped form the line. His 5:25 dispatch said the position on Cemetery Hill "cannot well be taken.
